question.text: A wire of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn></math> identical cells of negligible internal resistances are connected in series. Due to the current, the temperature of the wire is raised by <math> <mrow> <mo>Δ</mo> <mtext mathvariant="italic">T</mtext> </mrow> </math> <math><mrow><mo></mo> </mrow> </math>in a time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>t</mi></math>. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>N</mi></math> number of similar cells is now connected  in series with a wire of the same material and cross-section but of length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></math>. The temperature of the wire is raised by the same amount <math> <mrow> <mo>Δ</mo> <mtext mathvariant="italic">T</mtext> </mrow> </math> <math><mrow><mo></mo></mrow></math>in the same time. The value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>N</mi></math> is

solution.text:
In the first case,   3 E 2 R t = m s Δ T  ...(i)

                           H = V 2 R t

When length of the wire is doubled, resistance and mass both are doubled.
Therefore, in the second case,    

                  N E 2 2 R · t = 2 m s Δ T  ...(ii)

Dividing equation (ii) by (i), we get

                      N218=2 or N2=36 or N=6.
